sm: James Lindsay opens by saying the episode's title riffs on a Martin Luther work, and he says he does not endorse its anti-Semitism. He argues that the right needed a new mentality after the Bush and Obama years, and that MAGA under Trump provided it. He says a group calling itself the New Right, which he calls the woke right, claims that was not enough and wants a second, more radical transformation. In his telling this group includes Christian nationalists, post-liberals and national conservatives, is associated with Vance, and is not conservative. He calls this the scam and says it rests on a flood of lies.

Lindsay introduces mondialism, meaning one-world government, economy and democracy, with a left wing and a right wing. He says the left wing, which he links to neo-Marxism, tries to weaken strong Western countries so they will join a global order. He says the right wing, shown by the Bush doctrine of democracy building, tried to export the American system. He traces the history from Cold War containment and Reagan, through the Soviet collapse and the unipolar world, to Bush. He says Trump represents a break from mondialism.

Lindsay says Trump's rise interrupted the left mondialist plan that Obama and Clinton would have completed, which is why the World Economic Forum was so excited in 2016. He describes the right wing mondialists as democracy builders who muddled through Iraq and Afghanistan, and says this is what people mean by neocon and by the uniparty, though he calls the term too simple. He notes that Vance, Rubio and Trump each tap populist anger over lost jobs. He also explains the trade-off of open global trade, with cheaper goods but lost production jobs, citing Thomas Sowell.

Lindsay explains that the New Right blames a postwar liberal consensus that shut out nationalist and reactionary right-wing politics, as in Rusty Reno's book. He says that has a kernel of truth but is misnamed and overstated. He argues that if they saw mondialism as the real enemy, they would see that Trump already broke from it. He says the New Right attacks MAGA while claiming to be MAGA, spreading talk that Trump is bought or tied to Epstein. He calls Trump derangement syndrome a global operation by mondialists.

Lindsay concludes that Trump already supplied the needed new right, so a second, capital N New Right is unnecessary. He says it is not conservative or even American, and should be called national radicalism. He cites Vance calling himself part of a post-liberal right at an event for Patrick Deneen's book, Regime Change. He guesses that Vance's backers, such as Kevin Roberts, made big promises, and calls Vance a Manchurian candidate. He says the group borrows Carl Schmitt's friend and enemy idea and radicalizes youth through podcasts, with methods he compares to Maoist and Hitler Youth tactics.

Lindsay begins listing the lies, starting with a bait and switch on foreign policy. He says Trump's America First meant putting American interests first while cooperating with others, but groups like Nick Fuentes's Groypers turned it into America only isolationism. He says Trump's two promises, no new foreign wars and no Iranian nuclear weapon, contradicted each other, and Trump chose to stop Iran. He argues that ignoring hostile outside powers is naive, like ignoring robbers outside a house.

Lindsay says the New Right claims to back America First but constantly criticizes Trump's foreign policy, and he says that isolation would leave America divided and alone. The second lie is economic. He says America First economics meant putting American interests first, not autarky, and he questions a Trump cabinet remark that the era of cheap goods is over. He notes that complaints about tariffs and prices come from many sides, and that Trump's first term was good for manufacturing until COVID. He says the New Right instead offers family friendly socialism, or common good capitalism, citing Rubio.

Lindsay criticizes common good capitalism and the idea that the economy should work for the people, saying an economy cannot be controlled, only given rules. He also dislikes Trump's nationalizing of some industries, and he rejects Vance and Tucker Carlson's line that GDP is just a number. He says subsidies for stay at home mothers are an entitlement, though he thinks stable homes are better than welfare dependence. He then says make America great again is being swapped for America for Americans. He argues it divides citizens into heritage Americans and others, so the New Right decides who counts as real.

Lindsay says that some on the New Right call for deporting one hundred million or two hundred million people, which he says would include citizens and nearly every non-white citizen. He says this contradicts claims that they only oppose illegal immigration. He says they demand unity with them or they will use cancellation, state harassment, threats and mobbing. He adds that the hoped-for patriotic renewal became new patriotism: post-liberalism, Christian nationalism, Catholic integralism, and even national socialism. He cites Kevin Roberts's NatCon Jerusalem speech as an example.

Lindsay says Kevin Roberts, president of the Heritage Foundation, used the Jerusalem speech to demand unity around a new Republican party, as did the Fantastic Four speakers, including William Wolfe, Matt Peterson, Amanda Milius and Jonathan Keeper. He says these speeches told angry young people's critics to get on board or be punished. He lists the overlapping brands, from post-liberals and Schmittians to Christian nationalists, national conservatives and integralists. He says he would welcome a real Christian revival like Charlie Kirk's Make Heaven Full vision, but sees that hope being devoured.

Lindsay says the revival after Charlie Kirk's death was consumed by Tucker Carlson, Candace Owens and others, and replaced by a theology of glory, theonomy and theocracy, which he says pushes him away from the faith. He says the promise of alternative institutions became entryism. He names American Moment, which places young staffers in government, plus American Reformer and the Center for Baptist Leadership. He also says they took over or transformed Heritage, Claremont, Blaze Media, the Federalist, and others, while attacking those they cannot control, such as the Daily Wire.

Lindsay says the promised populism became aristopopulism, a new elitism in which the New Right replaces the old swamp and controls it, citing Vance remarks. He says the big tent became a controlled tent that excludes constitutional conservatives and critics like himself, and that Reagan's eleventh commandment became no enemies to the right. He gives Matt Walsh and Marjorie Taylor Greene as examples of being friendly with the Groypers. He then says the anti-woke movement became reaction with woke characteristics, and he notes the term woke light fits Rhino Republicans like Mike Pence.

Lindsay says the New Right uses woke tactics and critical theory, which is why he calls it the woke right, a reaction like the radical right after the French Revolution. He recaps the lies one by one, including America only foreign policy, isolationist common good economics, America for Americans, becoming and controlling the swamp, Christian nationalism instead of civic renewal, entryism, aristopopulism, a controlled tent, and unity criticism unity. He says they treat Trump and Vance as vehicles and are a second deviation from Trumpism. He concludes that they are a tyrannical movement and the right hand of the left.
